extracted.intended_audience: children's book authors, illustrators, editors, teachers, librarians, and readers interested in publishing/publishing_process
extracted.subtask_description: A publisher's editorial-blog collection where Scholastic editors describe working with authors, editorial decisions, and what they value in children's and young-adult books. Pieces cover picture books, middle-grade and YA novels, nonfiction reference, translations, and graphic novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial development process
rubrics_metrics.description: Our editors work with the author from idea to manuscript to finished page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes hands-on editorial involvement across the lifecycle of a book (idea development, manuscript editing, production). Appears as the general framing for the column (From the Editor's Desk) and underlies many of the individual pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to capture young readers' imaginations regardless of subject
rubrics_metrics.description: How a book about cotton can indeed capture the imaginations of young readers as much as any dragon or wizard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject matter need not be fantastical to engage children; narrative voice, presentation, and editorial shaping can make nonfiction as compelling as fiction (example: Up Before Daybreak).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional resonance / poignant message relevant to today
rubrics_metrics.description: A book full of historical treasures that hold a poignant message for today.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors value books that connect historical or specific material to contemporary relevance and emotional impact (example: Dear Miss Breed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to take chances on new or unconventional talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Lightning struck twice when she took a chance on publishing Wague Diakite, and then his truly gifted twelve-year-old daughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial risk-taking on unusual voices or debut creators is a recognized route to discovering distinctive work; editors note the payoff of such risks (example: I Lost My Tooth in Africa).

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketable / evocative title
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sometimes okay to judge a book by its name - and why Drums, Girls & Dangerous Pie is more than just a catchy title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong, memorable title can attract readers and signal tone/content; editors consider title as part of a book's appeal and market positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author–editor collaboration strengthens the book
rubrics_metrics.description: With Will of the Empress, I had the pleasure of working with two of my favorite people... their collaboration is stronger than ever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longstanding collaborative relationships between author and editor can improve continuity and quality across books; editors highlight the importance of teamwork and sustained editorial guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal themes and broad reader accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A book about a stray dog can hold a message for any reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that carry universal themes (family, identity, loss, belonging) can resonate across ages and backgrounds; picture-book topics should still aim for broad emotional relevance (example: A Dog’s Life).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing, imagination, and intellectual engagement (especially for children's mysteries)
rubrics_metrics.description: A richly detailed, fast-paced, imaginative, intelligent page-turner — a children's mystery that feels like a classic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For middle-grade mysteries, editors look for strong pacing, imaginative plotting, substantive details, and a sense of timelessness that keeps readers turning pages (example: Chasing Vermeer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential to generate buzz / commercial and cross-media interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Already the book is creating an incredible amount of 'buzz.' We know people are talking about it, because lots of people — including other publishers, and even movie companies! — have been calling us asking for copies to read!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors note and value early enthusiasm from industry and readers; commercial interest and buzz can be an informal criterion for a book's broader appeal and potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making classics accessible — retellings that are exciting and accessible for children
rubrics_metrics.description: Which offers beautifully illustrated retellings of Shakespeare's most famous works as exciting, accessible stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting classic works for children, success is measured by clarity, accessibility, and the ability to make canonical material feel vibrant and engaging (example: Tales from Shakespeare).

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-appropriate targeting and educational suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: A major new reference book, the Scholastic Children's Encyclopedia, for children in Grades 3-6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference and nonfiction titles should be clearly targeted to appropriate grade levels and curricular needs; editors consider suitability for specific age ranges and classroom use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration, visual design, and use of physical/prop elements in picture books
rubrics_metrics.description: Walter Wick is the photographer of the best-selling I SPY series... a search-and-find storybook for preschoolers. In this article, Walter's editor, Grace Maccarone, writes about the book, the author, and a prop named Seymour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For picture books and visually driven titles, illustration quality, layout, and inventive use of physical/visual props are central evaluative points; editorial work often integrates author and illustrator contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial handling of translations and internationally published works
rubrics_metrics.description: What distinguishes a good fantasy from a mediocre one, and how does an editor work on a novel originally published in another country?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors consider issues of translation, cultural context, and how to adapt voice and content for a new readership when acquiring and editing works first published abroad (example: The Singer of All Songs; The Legend of the Wandering King).

rubrics_metrics.name: Embracing new formats — graphic novels and imprint strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: We asked David Saylor... to tell us about the comic book saga, BONE, the first series from Scholastic’s new graphic novel imprint, GRAPHIX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial attention to format innovation (e.g., launching a graphic-novel imprint) and serial storytelling demonstrates a criterion of format suitability and strategic publishing decisions for reaching readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and historical relevance / use of biography and primary materials
rubrics_metrics.description: How a collection of letters to a librarian became a book full of historical treasures that hold a poignant message for today.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonfiction and biography that draw on primary sources or illuminate cultural/historical subjects are evaluated for their authenticity, relevance, and capacity to teach while engaging young readers (example: Dear Miss Breed).
